Re-elected Coun. Michael Moses said it has been a very fast and long four years. f715db01f20906d817838ab5c0aa742d.text: Rick Hansen and his teacher Harvey Glanville were in Williams Lake on Saturday, Oct. 17 for a 40th anniversary gala and screening of Hansen's Man In Motion. Welcoming ticket holders to an exclusive showing of Man In Motion: The Rick Hansen Story in Williams Lake on Saturday, Oct. 17 were mother and daughter Liz and Amanda Rennie. Providing live music during cocktail hour was Ebony, a teen string band with the Cariboo Chilcotin Youth Fiddle Society. Doing a live painting at a Oct. 17 gala and screening in Williams Lake supporting the Rick Hansen Foundation was artist Tiffany Jorgensen. Among those attending a recent 40th anniversary gala and screening in Williams Lake supporting the Rick Hansen Foundation was Leslie Campbell and her spouse. Rick Hansen was recently excited to be back home in Williams Lake for a gala event featuring an exclusive screening of his story that sparked an ongoing mission to create a more accessible and inclusive world. “This is where it all started,” Hansen told the *Williams Lake Tribune* on Saturday, Oct. 17 from the Gibraltar Room at the Cariboo Memorial Complex. Hansen was left paralyzed from the waist down in June 1973 after the vehicle he was riding lost control and rolled west of Williams Lake near Riske Creek. As he adapted to his new way of life, Hansen got involved in wheelchair sports establishing himself as a world class athlete. It was in March 1985 when Hansen and his team would set out on a landmark 26-month global wheelchair journey that is chronicled in the new documentary *Man in Motion: The Rick Hansen Story,* directed by Canadian filmmaker Adrian Buitenhuis and produced by Ryan Reynolds. 1e3d3562c55c4dfd617f590d7e2ac905.text: Change may have been in the air across B.C. this fall, but voter turnout certainly wasn’t. This past month, the citizens of the South Cariboo went to the polls twice, first for local municipal elections and then for a snap provincial election. Both elections have resulted in major change. In 100 Mile House, incumbent mayor Maureen Pinkney has been replaced by political newcomer David Jurek, alongside two new councillors. Provincially, our own MLA, Lorne Doerkson, secured re-election and is now the premier-elect, with his party, the Conservative Party of B.C., set to enjoy a majority government with over 60 seats in Victoria. The results of both elections will directly impact our lives and the direction of our community and, in the case of Doerkson, the province for the next four years. Voting’s power was on full display. Yet, voter turnout was not. Here in 100 Mile House, only 40 per cent of eligible voters cast a ballot for mayor and council. Province-wide on Saturday, Oct. 24, around 48 per cent of the electorate cast ballots, down sharply from just over 58 per cent two years ago. When more people choose not to vote than to vote, do we truly have a democracy? Had these people voted, would the outcomes have been the same, or would they have been wildly different? Sadly, we’ll never know. Voter apathy, truly, is the bane of a democratic society. While our first-past-the-post system isn’t perfect, people choosing not to engage with it doesn’t fix it; it just entrenches it. There is a notion among some eligible voters that nothing ever changes and that voting is meaningless. If that were the case, why did our forefathers fight so hard for the privilege? Why do people who don’t live in democratic societies fight for the right to vote? Why do the powerful spend so much money influencing the outcome of elections, if it doesn’t matter? c9de93c1062636154eb2dc8879d3c11d.text: Athletes are arriving in Kelowna for 2026 Skate Canada International (SCI). The best in figure skating across the globe will be competing at Prospera Place Oct. 30 to Nov. 1. Kelowna is the second stop on the SCI Grand Prix series and athletes will be competing for points toward qualification for the Grand Prix Final. Stephen Gogolev is representing Canada in the men’s event. The reigning Canadian champion finished in the top five at both the Olympic Winter Games and the World Championships in his 2025-26 season. In the women’s event, four-time Canadian champion Madeline Schizas will be making her sixth appearance. Two Canadian duos will compete in the pair’s event. Lia Pereira and Trennt Michaud aim for another gold after winning the Nebelhorn Trophy in Germany in September. The reigning junior world champions, Ava Kemp and Yohnatan Elizarov will be making their Grand Prix debut in Kelowna. Canadian couple Marie-Jade Lauriault and Romain Le Gac will be competing in the ice dance event, coming off of a 2026 Canadian Championship bronze medal win. The contest begins Friday, Oct. 30 at 6 p.m. with the men’s short program. The opening ceremony will follow at 7:30 p.m. Medal ceremonies for the men’s and pair’s events will take place at the end of the day on Saturday, Oct. 31. Medal ceremonies for the women’s and ice dance events will take place at the conclusion of the competition on Sunday, Nov. 1. Families are invited to check out Skate Fest Oct. 30-31 outside Prospera Place. The fan event will includes games and activities, vendors, live music and a Halloween treat. Find the event schedule, information on the athletes and tickets by visiting skatecanada.ca.

a464defcbef23fcda7d4c67e816c84f5.text: For the second time, an Armstrong fast food manager has lost an appeal related to his sexual exploitation of a 16-year-old employee. Surjit Singh was 26 years old at the time of the offences, for which he was sentenced to 13 months jail in 2024. After losing an appeal of the conviction back in April, he requested that the B.C. Court of Appeal replace the jail sentence with a conditional sentence served in the community. An appeal court panel dismissed this second appeal, according to a decision released Oct. 2, having found the trial judge made no error in landing on a 13-month jail sentence. Singh became the temporary manager at the fast food restaurant in the summer of 2021. The victim in the case had already worked there for several years and was 15 at the time. Singh knew her age and had researched the age of consent in Canada online. He brought a cake to her home on her 16th birthday. The relationship became sexual, and sexual contact occurred over a two month period at the restaurant, in Singh’s car and in his apartment. The relationship ended when a friend of the victim discovered text messages between her and Singh. The girl’s mother approached restaurant managers and Singh was suspended. He then left the province and was later arrested and brought back to B.C., where he spent eight days in pre-sentence custody. Singh was convicted of sexual exploitation in May 2024. He was acquitted of other charges including sexual assault, as the judge accepted that the relationship was mutual and there was no evidence of grooming. Consent was not at issue in the case; instead it was about Singh’s position of authority. In the April ruling, the court noted Singh held enough control over the victim that “when he wanted to be able to access her cellphone and delete text messages, she let him do that.” It found he had significant control over shift schedules and quantities, and other aspects of the victim’s working life. An Oct. 28 press release from the Kamloops RCMP said the “serious collision” required multiple emergency responders to attend the scene after a car went off the road and down an embankment. “On October 27, 2026, at approximately 6:40 p.m., police received a cell phone crash detection and received multiple reports that a vehicle had gone off Highway 1 near the 3900-block by Cherry Creek,” police said. “The grey Ford Focus was reported to be travelling East on Highway 1 and went off road to the right and then down an embankment of approximately 60ft.” Police noted that Kamloops and Tk’emlúps Rural RCMP detachment frontline officers attended, along with multiple BC Ambulance units, Kamloops Fire Rescue, and New Afton Mine Rescue. BC Highway Patrol also attended to assist with the investigation. Cpl. Dana Napier, spokesperson for the Tk’emlúps Rural RCMP detachment, commented on the incident. “There were five occupants in the vehicle, all five occupants were transported to the hospital where two remain in critical condition,” she said. “The cause of the crash is still being investigated, however, at this time, impairment was not a factor in the crash.” RCMP said anyone who may have been on the highway near the time of the incident and who has dash camera footage of the grey Ford Focus going off-road is asked to contact the Tk’emlúps Rural RCMP detachment at 250-314-1800 and cite file 2026-36059.

72d0cb53d314bf9ecf33a216b0b433c8.text: Darker drives, greater risks: How not ‘falling back’ should change driving habits in B.C. | Williams Lake Tribune Darker drives, greater risks: How not ‘falling back’ should change driving habits in B.C. A B.C.-based safety organization says roads in the province are about to get more dangerous for professional drivers, not to mention motorists who don’t drive for a living. With clocks not “falling back” an hour this weekend, B.C. drivers will spend mornings in more darkness and low light. Road Safety at Work, which aims to improve the safety of people who drive for work or work at the roadside, urges employers and drivers to prepare for reduced visibility and fatigue, and also consider changing their ways this winter. Early Sunday (Nov. 1), B.C. will remain on permanent Daylight Saving Time, meaning sunrise will arrive later this winter. More work trips, morning commutes and school drop-offs will take place in darkness, at a time of year when rain, fog and snow are more common. “Employers need to assess how changing conditions affect workers who drive for work and put appropriate controls in place to reduce those risks,” urges Todd McDonald, head of prevention services at WorkSafeBC. Science says prolonged morning darkness affects natural sleep cycles and may contribute to driver fatigue. Warning signs of fatigue include frequent yawning, difficulty concentrating, drifting within a lane, sore eyes, and difficulty remembering the last few kilometres. “The roads you drive may be familiar but the risks are changing” with permanent Daylight Saving Time, cautions Trace Acres, program director for Road Safety at Work. “In darkness or low light, it’s harder to spot hazards on the road and react.” Employers can help by adjusting schedules that call for driving early in the morning, at night or for long periods, if possible, Acres says. This fall and winter, drivers should slow down when visibility is reduced and leave more distance between vehicles, Road Safety at Work

c466d6f17d5c85b9caf739460559362d.text: Silver Star Mountain Resort has been named the fifth best ski resort in North America in Condé Nast Traveller's 2026 Readers' Choice Awards, published in October 2026. North Okanagan residents know SilverStar Mountain Resort to be a winter paradise rivalling any other. They might be surprised at how many people from far and wide feel the same way about their local ski resort. SilverStar has been ranked fifth among the best ski resorts in North America in Condé Nast Traveller’s 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards, earning a score of 93.26 out of 100. The North American ranking lists 15 resorts. Deer Valley in Utah placed first with a score of 97.78, followed by Sun Valley in Idaho, Vail in Colorado and Whistler Blackcomb in B.C. With Silver Star in fifth, B.C. holds two of the top five places. Mount Washington on Vancouver Island placed ninth, giving the province three resorts on the list. The only other Canadian resort to crack the list was Lake Louise, Alta., which placed 15th. “A village that people live in year-round, alpine runs that still feel like yours on a busy day, and 105 kilometres of pristine Nordic trails. That’s what carries our story further than any campaign could,” said Michael Benedek, executive director of Destination Silver Star. Silver Star’s alpine terrain covers 3,303 skiable acres and 133 runs, with 760 metres of vertical drop. The village sits at 1,609 metres and offers ski-in, ski-out access from its colourful pedestrian village that is home to year-round residents. Silver Star’s Nordic trails connect with Sovereign Lake Nordic Centre to form 105 kilometres of groomed cross-country and skate ski trails, one of the largest combined alpine and Nordic networks in North America. The mountain receives an average of 700 centimetres of snow each year and is 22 kilometres from downtown Vernon in the North Okanagan. 9bd686aa3e9452f593790d4089e035d0.text: The RCMP is seeking public assistance in locating Chelcey Hodder, 43, who is wanted on Canada-wide warrant for failing to return to a facility as ordered. Hodder has been missing since Oct. 23, and is believed to be in the Hope area or travelling to Kamloops. Coquitlam RCMP is asking for the public’s help in locating a woman wanted on a Canada-wide warrant who is believed to be in the Hope or Kamloops areas. Chelcey Hodder, 43, was last seen at 2:30 p.m. in the area of ƛ̓éxətəm Regional Park in Coquitlam on Oct. 23. She is wanted on a warrant of committal after failing to return to her facility as ordered. The Coquitlam RCMP Investigational Support Team tracked Hodder to Hope, and it is believed she is either still in the Hope area or is travelling to Kamloops. The police say to not approach Hodder if she is seen. After talking with the male driver, Lamb said officers determined he was prohibited from driving. “The male was arrested and later released to attend court at a future date,” Lamb said. “The ATV was impounded and the male was also served a violation ticket for no insurance.” Sometime overnight on Oct. 22, a commercial property was broken into on Horse Lake Road. On May 26, 2026 the founder of the Cow Moose Moose Sign Project received an award commemorating him being a finalist of the inaugural Dr. Valerius Geist Conservation Legacy Award. It was launched by Hunters for BC to recognize those who continue the legacy of the renowned scientist who was also a hunter, storyteller, naturalist and mentor by making meaningful contributions to wildlife and habitat conservation across North America. Simmons was nominated by Hunters for BC vice president Dave Ryder who retired from the B.C.-based, hunter-led non-profit conservation organization earlier this month. As one of seven distinguished finalists from across Canada and the U.S. Simmons was presented with a hand-engraved glass award he said he received on his 72nd birthday by Purolator. “It took about 30 pictures,” Dan remarked of finally getting just the right one of him smiling with his wife Vivian as they held the award with Horsefly Lake in the background. 58a4bb201e525246ae19a15e4b5640f3.text: Vancouver Canucks centre Elias Pettersson fires a shot during NHL action Thursday, Oct 29, 2026 against the San Jose Sharks at the SAP Center in San Jose, Calif. Will Smith scored a pair of goals, leading the San Jose Sharks to a come-from-behind 3-2 win over the visiting Vancouver Canucks in NHL action Thursday at the SAP Center in San Jose, Calif. Mason Marchment also scored for the Sharks (7-6-1), who trailed 2-0 midway through the third period. Yaroslav Askarov made 23 saves to earn the win in goal. Drew O’Connor and Liam Öhgren scored for the Canucks (3-11-1), who ended a 10-game losing skid Tuesday in Anaheim. Leevi Merilainen stopped 21 of 24 shots and took the loss for Vancouver. O’Connor scored the lone goal of the first period, driving to the net and knocking home a rebound off a shot from centre Elias Pettersson at 13:21. O’Connor now has two goals on the season and Pettersson is on a six-game point-scoring streak. Öhgren upped the lead to 2-0 with just 1:04 left in the second period, ripping a shot past Askarov from about 20 feet out near the right faceoff circle for his fourth of the year. Smith pulled San Jose within one eight minutes into the second on the power play, moving in from the point and beating Merilainen from the top of the right circle with his fifth of the season. With 9:21 left in the period, Smith struck again, taking a nifty pass from Macklin Celebrini and beating Merilainen for his second of the game. Just 11 seconds after that, the Sharks controlled the faceoff and Marchment moved down the left side and fired a shot through Merilainen to give San Jose a 3-2 lead. On a late power play in the third, the Canucks pulled Merilainen to create a 6-on-4 situation but were unable to convert and the Sharks hung on for the win. c9397c67db640a21667ac8866300603f.text: Community Foundation North Okanagan presents $10,000 to Okanagan Indian Band Chief and Council for food security work after the Bradley Creek wildfire, September 8, 2026. Support continues to make its way to people affected by the Bradley Creek wildfire near Vernon. Community Foundation North Okanagan (CFNO) has granted $55,000 from the Wildfire Response 2026 Fund to 13 local organizations supporting people displaced by the blaze that rapidly spread on Aug. 1. The grants are funding food security, mental health support help for families who were evacuated or lost property, animal rescue, and services for newcomers and Indigenous residents. The fund was established on Aug. 5 as a trusted local place to give after the Bradley Creek wildfire forced evacuations across the North Okanagan. Since then, 471 donors have contributed $348,716. The fund is still open and more granting is planned, at cfno.org/wildfire-response-2026. This first round of grants went to organizations already on the ground, in direct contact with people who had been evacuated or had lost homes. “Granting locally means support arrives through people who already know their neighbours and can direct it where it will do the most good,” the CFNO said. **Okanagan Indian Band:** $23,000 across three grants. An early $3,000 went out on Aug. 7 for immediate needs. In September, CFNO presented $10,000 to Chief and Council for food security work, helping replace food lost during evacuations and restock fridges, freezers and pantries, and a further $10,000 to the What Happens Upstream youth conference, supporting young people affected by the fire. Donors who wished to support OKIB programs directly were also able to give through the OKIB Fund. **School District 22:** $10,000. Supporting 21 families across five schools who were displaced by the fire. The district has been helping families purchase clothing, household necessities and groceries, and has made breakfasts, lunches, snacks and take-home meals

A woman who spent nearly a lifetime dedicated to caring for and supporting those with disabilities is being fondly remembered. Isabella Dorothy Alexander died Oct. 1, 2026 at the age of 87. Better known as Dorothy, her contributions to the Vernon area touched countless lives and continue to be felt through the community. “Dorothy Alexander was not only a remarkable advocate for persons with disabilities in our community, but also a true pioneer whose vision and dedication helped shape the services and opportunities available today,” said Ryan Cucheron, chief executive officer of Venture Living – formerly Venture Training, which Alexander was on the founding board of. While born in Manitoba, Alexander grew up in Spallumcheen’s Hullcar area and went to Armstrong Elementary School. After high school she furthered her education and began a lifelong commitment to helping others. “Dorothy became a passionate advocate for people with disabilities, working to ensure they had opportunities to learn, participate, and live with dignity,” her obituary reads. Playing an important role in the early development of services for people with disabilities in Vernon, in 1958 Alexander started at My School providing education and activities for 10 children with disabilities (and that number continued to grow). Under her leadership, the program flourished, eventually expanding and relocating to what is now Venture Living’s main location on Alexis Park Drive, according to Cucheron. “During the 1960s and 1970s, Dorothy used approaches that were truly groundbreaking for their time,” he said. “While community inclusion may seem like a natural expectation today, her efforts to bring individuals with disabilities into the community challenged the prevailing attitudes of institutionalization. She believed strongly that individuals with disabilities deserved opportunities

Under the legislation, the Chief Election Officer, a candidate in the election, or any four electors may apply to the court for a determination, the *Now-Leader* is told. “Any application must be filed within 30 days of the certification of the election results, which is November 20,” Surrey Schools says in an email. “As a result, the District cannot comment on what Garry Thind’s election as an MLA means for filling the final Board seat or the possibility of any byelection. That will depend on whether a court application is made and, if so, how the court rules.” The district statement adds: “Initial cost estimates provided to Surrey Schools by the City of Surrey place the cost of a byelection at approximately $840,000. Fire crews on scene of blaze at the Creative Studies building on UBCO campus. A fire that broke out at the Creative and Critical Studies building at UBC Okanagan has been contained, according to the Kelowna Fire Department (KFD). The blaze, which started at around 12:30 p.m. on Thursday, Oct. 29, was extinguished due to the efforts of the KFD, who deployed 30 firefighters, five engines and two ladder trucks to the scene. Deputy Fire Chief Larry Watkinson told reporters at the scene that the preliminary investigations suggest the fire was started due to construction work on the roof of the building. “Behind the cladding is an insulated foam packaging, and it caught fire. It ran up the inside of the cladding which got into the structure, and that’s how the fire started,” Watkinson said. He added that no one was found inside the building as fire crews arrived, and no students or firefighters were injured. The deputy fire chief said the fire was contained and there was “very limited” impact to any of the classrooms in the connecting building. Still, the original structure suffered some smoke and water damage. A blaze in the roof of the Creative and Critical Studies building, has caused an evacuation as fire crews continue to douse the smoke and flame. All classes and exams in the building are cancelled until further notice. Additional student supports are available at students.ok.ubc.ca/support/support-for-unanticipated-circumstances. A large fire is burning inside the Creative Studies building on the University of British Columbia Okanagan campus. Huge plumes of smoke could be seen rising from the building just after 12 p.m. According to those on campus, flames can also be seen coming from the building.
